newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar tightens security ahead of Gulf summit.
newsitem.headline: Qatar tightens security ahead of Gulf summit.

text.p: Qatar is stepping up security ahead of a December summit of Gulf Arab leaders in Doha in the wake of an attempt to blow up a government building, a senior official said on Tuesday.

Helicopters on security exercises hovered over the capital and naval patrols cleared the bay of dhows. Residents said night patrols and security at all government offices and diplomatic missions were being beefed up.
"In the immediate sense, it (the alert) has been triggered by the incident of last Saturday...but, anyway, we were preparing for the coming summit," the official said.

He was referring to what he called an "attempt by some miscreants to plant a crude device outside the offices of Immigration, Passport and Naturalisation with an intent to damage it and create confusion".
An anonymous caller had telephoned the police to say a bomb had been planted on the premises. The device was defused.
No arrests have been announced in connection with the incident, but officials said many people had been interrogated.

"The incident could have been dismissed as inconsequential or at best as a childish misdemeanor in normal circumstances. But coming as it does ahead of the (Gulf Cooperation Council) GCC summit we cannot take it lightly...the so-called crazy supporters of the ex-ruler might try to make trouble and confusion," said the official who requested anonymity.
Qatar's former emir, Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad al-Thani, was ousted by his eldest son Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani in a bloodless coup in June last year.
Calling himself legitimate ruler of Qatar, he has vowed to return to power in the oil and gas-rich state.
The deposed emir returned to the Gulf last December and toured GCC states in an attempt to muster support for his bid to return to Qatar.

Last February, the government said it foiled a plot to topple Sheikh Hamad. A Qatari official said at the time that some of those arrested were members of a personal army raised by Sheikh Khalifa during his rule.
Qatar has filed a case in a local court and started legal proceedings in eight countries to recover more than $3.5 billion of state funds alleged to have been stolen by the former emir.
